title: 2009 AMC 12B Problem 24
statement:
For how many values of \(x\) in \([0, \pi]\) is \(\sin^{-1}(\sin 6x) = \cos^{-1}(\cos x)?\)

Note: The functions \(\sin^{-1} = \arcsin\) and \(\cos^{-1} = \arccos\) denote inverse trigonometric functions.

solutions.text:
On \([0, \pi],\ \cos^{-1}(\cos x) = x.\) Since \(\sin^{-1}\) takes values in \([-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}],\) any solution requires \(x \in [0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}],\) where the equation becomes \(\sin 6x = \sin x.\)

The equation \(\sin6x=\sin x\) holds exactly when \[ \begin{aligned} 6x&=x+2k\pi, \\ \text{or}\qquad 6x&=\pi-x+2k\pi \end{aligned} \] for some integer \(k.\)

The first family gives \(x=\tfrac{2k\pi}{5},\) contributing \(0\) and \(\tfrac{2\pi}{5}.\) The second gives \(x=\tfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{7},\) contributing \(\tfrac\pi7\) and \(\tfrac{3\pi}{7}.\) Hence there are \(4\) solutions in \([0,\tfrac\pi2].\)

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: On \([0, \pi],\ \cos^{-1}(\cos x) = x,\) and the left side lies in \([-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}],\) so any solution needs \(x \in [0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]\)
Since \(\sin\) is one-to-one on \([-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}],\) the equation reduces to \(\sin 6x = \sin x\) on \([0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]\)
